prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The camera wearer’s forearms, hands, carrot, and knife are the nearest geometry, roughly 0.2–0.6 m away; the table edges and nearby chairs are approximately 0.7–1.5 m away, with the floor and farther furniture extending to roughly 1–3 m. The hands and tools remain in front of and below the camera, while the table is above them in the image and the chairs lie farther ahead or to the sides; no separate person or face is clearly visible, so facing direction and gaze cannot be determined. Across frames 1–3 the tools stay near the center and at similar depth, frame 4 brings the raised left forearm and carrot especially close, and frame 5 returns both hands and tools toward the center-right at arm’s reach. The depth map makes near/far layering, contact-level proximity, and occlusion by the arms much clearer than RGB, but object boundaries merge around the hands and knife, and brightness varies enough that these metric distances are only rough monocular estimates.
descriptions.segmentation: The map separates the camera wearer’s visible arms and hands as person regions and identifies nearby tool-sized objects, including the carrot and knife, all within roughly 0.2–0.6 m and overlapping or touching one another near the lower-middle foreground. No distinct second person is reliably segmented, and no head or face is visible, so neither another person’s position nor anyone’s facing direction or gaze can be established. Over time, the foreground person mask shifts from left/center to center, then stretches diagonally upward in frame 4 as the carrot moves higher and slightly right, before returning to a compact center-right configuration in frame 5; the arms partly occlude the tools throughout. Segmentation clarifies which image regions belong to the foreground body versus small objects, but labels such as remote, toothbrush, and laptop appear inconsistent with the RGB, the knife is missed or fragmented in some frames, and most furniture and room surfaces are left unlabelled.
descriptions.pose: The pose map localizes only the camera wearer’s hands: magenta hand skeletons appear in the lower-left or lower-center in frame 1, spread across the central foreground in frame 2, cluster near the center in frame 3, contract around the center-right raised hand region in frame 4, and appear near the upper-right foreground in frame 5. These keypoints show the hands remaining within approximately 0.2–0.6 m of the camera and close to each other and the tools, while revealing changes in finger arrangement and wrist orientation that are difficult to distinguish in RGB. No yellow body skeleton, head, face, or separate person pose is visible, so body orientation, gaze, distances to other people, and whether anything is within another person’s reach cannot be inferred. The hand skeletons are partly unreliable where fingers, carrot, knife, and hands overlap: connections bunch together, some joints appear displaced or missing, and the map provides no direct depth or room-layout information.
